q: Which one of the following is a base unit of the SI?
x: The kelvin is the SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature. The newton, joule and coulomb are derived units (the coulomb is built from the base unit ampere: 1 C = 1 A s).

q: In the SI, the radian is the unit of:
x: The radian is the supplementary unit of plane angle. The steradian is the supplementary unit of solid angle, which is the most common mix-up.

q: The newton expressed in SI base units is:
x: F = ma, so 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m s⁻² = 1 kg m s⁻². kg m² s⁻² is the joule and kg m s⁻¹ is the unit of momentum.

q: A car moves at 72 km h⁻¹. Its speed in m s⁻¹ is:
x: 72 km h⁻¹ = 72 × 1000 m ÷ 3600 s = 20 m s⁻¹. Multiplying by 3.6 instead of dividing gives about 259 m s⁻¹.

q: The wavelength of a green light is 500 nm. In metres, written in scientific notation, this is:
x: 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m, so 500 nm = 500 × 10⁻⁹ m = 5 × 10⁻⁷ m. Writing 5 × 10⁻⁹ m forgets to move the decimal point for the 500.

q: The density of aluminium is 2.7 g cm⁻³. In SI units this is:
x: 1 g = 10⁻³ kg and 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³, so 1 g cm⁻³ = 10⁻³/10⁻⁶ = 10³ kg m⁻³ and 2.7 g cm⁻³ = 2700 kg m⁻³. Converting only the cm³ gives 2.7 × 10⁶.

q: The pascal, the SI unit of pressure, expressed in base units is:
x: Pressure = force ÷ area = (kg m s⁻²) ÷ m² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻². kg m s⁻² is the newton itself, forgetting to divide by the area.

q: A copper wire is 2 km long and has a cross-sectional area of 0.5 mm². The volume of the copper in the wire is:
x: 0.5 mm² = 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ m² and 2 km = 2000 m, so V = 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ × 2000 = 1 × 10⁻³ m³. Taking 1 mm² as 10⁻³ m² gives 1 m³; leaving the length in km gives 10⁻⁶ m³.

q: The number 0.0000456 written in scientific notation is:
x: The decimal point moves 5 places to the right to give 4.56, so the number is 4.56 × 10⁻⁵. Counting only the zeros after the decimal point (4) gives the wrong power 10⁻⁴.

q: A 2 kW heater is switched on for 30 minutes. The electrical energy it uses, in megajoules, is:
x: E = Pt = 2000 W × (30 × 60 s) = 3.6 × 10⁶ J = 3.6 MJ. Leaving the time as 30 (not seconds) gives 0.06 MJ, and using one hour gives 7.2 MJ.

q: A screw gauge reads 0.02 mm when its jaws are closed with nothing between them. The error this causes in every reading is:
o: A percentage error that averages out
An error caused only by the observer
x: A zero error shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction, so it is a systematic error. It is removed by subtracting the zero error, not by averaging.

q: Random errors in a measurement can best be reduced by:
o: Applying a zero correction to each reading
Taking the mean of several repeated readings
Using an instrument with a larger least count
x: Random errors scatter readings on both sides of the true value, so averaging many readings reduces their effect. A zero correction removes a systematic error, not a random one.

q: A length is recorded as 25.0 ± 0.5 cm. Its percentage uncertainty is:
x: Percentage uncertainty = (0.5 ÷ 25.0) × 100% = 2%. Leaving out the × 100 gives 0.02, and quoting the absolute uncertainty as a percentage gives 0.5%.

q: Two lengths, 10.2 ± 0.1 cm and 5.1 ± 0.1 cm, are added. The total length with its uncertainty is:
x: When quantities are added (or subtracted), their absolute uncertainties are added: 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2 cm. Taking the uncertainty of only one length gives ± 0.1 cm.

q: The length of a rectangle is measured with a 1% uncertainty and its width with a 2% uncertainty. The percentage uncertainty in its area is:
x: For a product, the percentage uncertainties are added: 1% + 2% = 3%. Averaging them gives 1.5%, and taking only the larger one gives 2%.

q: The radius of a sphere is measured with an uncertainty of 2%. The percentage uncertainty in its calculated volume is:
x: V = (4/3)πr³, so the percentage uncertainty in V is 3 × 2% = 6%; the constant 4/3 π has no uncertainty. Treating the power as 2 (as for area) gives 4%.

q: The mass of a trolley is measured with a 1% uncertainty and its speed with a 2% uncertainty. The percentage uncertainty in its kinetic energy, ½mv², is:
x: Percentage uncertainty in KE = (% in m) + 2 × (% in v) = 1% + 2 × 2% = 5%. Forgetting that v is squared gives 3%; the factor ½ adds no uncertainty.

q: The time for 20 oscillations of a pendulum is 40.0 s, measured with a stopwatch of least count 0.1 s. The time period with its uncertainty is:
x: T = 40.0 ÷ 20 = 2.000 s, and the uncertainty is also divided by the number of oscillations: 0.1 ÷ 20 = 0.005 s. Keeping the full 0.1 s gives 2.0 ± 0.1 s.

q: g is found from g = 4π²l/T². The length l has a 1% uncertainty and the period T has a 0.5% uncertainty. The percentage uncertainty in g is:
x: % in g = % in l + 2 × % in T = 1% + 2 × 0.5% = 2%. Uncertainties add even though T is in the denominator; forgetting the square gives 1.5%, and subtracting gives 0.5% or 0%.

q: A voltmeter always reads 0.2 V more than the true voltage. If many readings are taken and averaged, the mean value will:
o: Be free of the 0.2 V error
x: A constant offset is a systematic error: every reading is 0.2 V too high, so their mean is also 0.2 V too high. Averaging reduces only random errors; this one needs a correction or recalibration.

q: The number of significant figures in 0.00520 is:
x: Leading zeros only place the decimal point and are not significant; the trailing zero after the decimal point is. So 5, 2 and the final 0 are significant: 3 figures. Dropping the final zero gives 2.

q: The number of significant figures in 6.020 × 10²³ is:
x: In scientific notation only the digits of the number in front count: 6, 0, 2 and the final 0, so 4 significant figures. The power of ten does not add figures.

q: Two measurements are P = 50.0 ± 0.5 cm and Q = 2.00 ± 0.05 cm. Their percentage uncertainties are:
x: P: 0.5 ÷ 50.0 × 100% = 1%. Q: 0.05 ÷ 2.00 × 100% = 2.5%. So P has the larger absolute uncertainty but the smaller percentage uncertainty; quoting the absolute values as percentages is the common slip.

q: A length of 1.5 m is multiplied by a width of 3.42 m. The area written to the correct number of significant figures is:
x: 1.5 × 3.42 = 5.13, and a product keeps as many significant figures as the least precise factor (1.5 has 2), so 5.1 m². Keeping all the calculator digits gives 5.13 m².

q: Three lengths, 12.11 m, 0.3 m and 8.006 m, are added. The sum written correctly is:
x: 12.11 + 0.3 + 8.006 = 20.416 m. In addition the result keeps as many decimal places as the term with the fewest (0.3 has one), so 20.4 m.

q: The value 0.06784 rounded to three significant figures is:
x: The first three significant figures are 6, 7, 8; the next digit is 4, which is less than 5, so the 8 stays: 0.0678. Rounding up to 0.0679 is wrong because the dropped digit is below 5.

q: The radius of a disc is measured as 2.50 cm. Taking π = 3.14, its area written to the correct number of significant figures is:
x: A = πr² = 3.14 × 2.50² = 3.14 × 6.25 = 19.625 cm². Both 3.14 and 2.50 have 3 significant figures, so the area is 19.6 cm². Keeping all digits gives 19.625 cm².

q: A vernier callipers of least count 0.01 cm shows that a rod's diameter is exactly two and three-tenths of a centimetre. The reading should be recorded as:
x: A reading is recorded to the least count of the instrument, here the second decimal place of a centimetre: 2.30 cm. Writing 2.3 cm throws away a measured zero; 2.300 cm claims more precision than the instrument gives.

q: A box has a mass of 2.3 kg. Two coins of masses 20.15 g and 20.17 g are put into it. The total mass, written correctly, is:
x: In kilograms: 2.3 + 0.02015 + 0.02017 = 2.34032 kg. The sum keeps the fewest decimal places of the terms, one decimal place from 2.3 kg, so the total is 2.3 kg. The coins are too light to change the recorded value.

q: A distance of 3200 m is known to exactly three significant figures. It is best written as:
x: Scientific notation shows the significant figures without doubt: three figures means 3.20 × 10³ m. 3.2 × 10³ m has only two, and 3.200 × 10³ m has four.

q: The dimensions of force are:
x: F = ma = [M][LT⁻²] = [MLT⁻²]. [ML²T⁻²] is energy, [MLT⁻¹] is momentum and [ML⁻¹T⁻²] is pressure.

q: Which pair of quantities has the same dimensions?
x: Work = force × distance and torque = force × moment arm, both [ML²T⁻²]. Momentum is [MLT⁻¹] and force [MLT⁻²]; power is energy per second.

q: The energy of a photon is E = hf, where f is its frequency. The dimensions of Planck's constant h are:
x: h = E/f = [ML²T⁻²] ÷ [T⁻¹] = [ML²T⁻¹]. Multiplying by [T⁻¹] instead of dividing gives [ML²T⁻³], the dimensions of power.

q: Here u and v are velocities, a is acceleration, s is distance and t is time. Which equation is dimensionally incorrect?
x: at² has dimensions [LT⁻²][T²] = [L], a length, which cannot be added to a velocity [LT⁻¹]. In each of the other equations every term has the same dimensions.

q: The displacement of an oscillating body is x = x₀ sin ωt, where t is time. The dimensions of ω are:
x: The angle ωt inside the sine must be dimensionless, so ω = 1/t has dimensions [T⁻¹]. Giving ω the dimensions of time gives [T].

q: An equation is found to be dimensionally correct. Which conclusion is justified?
o: It must be wrong if it contains a numerical constant
It must contain only base quantities
It may still be wrong, because dimensions cannot check pure-number constants such as ½ or 2π
x: Dimensional homogeneity is necessary but not sufficient: s = ut + at² is dimensionally correct but has the wrong factor (it should be ½at²). Dimensionless constants are invisible to the check.

q: Assume the period T of a simple pendulum depends only on its length l and on g. Dimensional analysis gives:
x: Put T = k lᵃ gᵇ: [T] = [L]ᵃ[LT⁻²]ᵇ, so a + b = 0 and −2b = 1, giving b = −½ and a = ½. Hence T ∝ √(l/g). The ratio l/g alone has dimensions [T²], not [T].

q: Stokes' law gives the drag force on a sphere of radius r moving at speed v through a fluid as F = 6πηrv. The dimensions of the viscosity η are:
x: η = F/(6πrv) = [MLT⁻²] ÷ ([L][LT⁻¹]) = [ML⁻¹T⁻¹]; 6π is a pure number. Dividing by v only gives [MT⁻¹], and dividing by r only gives [MT⁻²].

q: For a spring, F = kx, where F is the force and x the extension. The dimensions of the spring constant k are:
x: k = F/x = [MLT⁻²] ÷ [L] = [MT⁻²]. Forgetting to divide by the extension leaves [MLT⁻²], the dimensions of force.

q: The velocity of a particle is given by v = at + b/(t + c), where t is time. The dimensions of the constant b are:
x: c is added to t, so c has dimensions [T]. Then b/[T] must be a velocity [LT⁻¹], so b = [LT⁻¹][T] = [L]. Taking b itself as a velocity gives [LT⁻¹].
